image_description:
**1. Chart type**  
- **Choropleth map** of U.S. states.

**2. Layout techniques**  
- Uses **geographic layout** (states positioned by location on a U.S. map).
- No faceting, stacking, or small multiples.
- Uses **color bins** (discrete legend categories) to encode value ranges.

**3. Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Geographic region/position (state shapes on the U.S. map) |
| Number of banned books | Quantitative | Fill color of each state, grouped into ordinal legend bins |
| Banned-book count range (0, 1–10, 11–100, 101–500, 501–1,000, 1,001–3,000, 3,001–6,000) | Ordinal | Color/hue categories in the legend and state fills |
| Time period: July to December 2023 | Temporal | Subtitle text/label |

comments.raw_comment: I noticed a few things in the What’s Going On in This Graph. The graph analyzes banned books in each state and the data was collected from July to December 2023. The state of Florida has the highest number of banned books throughout the United States in 2023; meanwhile Alabama, Delaware, Connecticut, Alaska, Arizona, Montana, and Nevada have zero banned books from July - December 2023. I wonder what regulations and laws have been implemented in Florida that have led to the banning of 3,001 - 6,000 books. Are there groups that go through and take votes on the true meaning of the books, or is a book automatically banned if it doesn’t meet a certain requirement? This relates specifically to me and my community because throughout my years in the garfieldre2 district in Colorado, there are books that my classmates and I have read and evaluated in class that are now banned. I think a catchy title that could be used to address this graph would be, What’s your Favorite Book?

comments.raw_comment:
What appears at the top of the article is not a graph. 
    
    It is a map: a choropleth map, to be specific: a powerful tool that allows those reading it to discern regional patterns, or the lack of them, in the variable being mapped. 
    
    We see them every election night, when we watch as states flip from some neutral tone to red or blue, showing a Reblican or a Democratic victory in that state  Did you ever once hear the even most ill-informed of election night pundits refer to those maps as graphs?
    
    Any data collected on a state-by-state basis can be mapped the same way: ditto data collected county by county, district by district, country by country, etc. Commonly a range of dark to light tones of a single color distinguishes places with higher to lower unemployment rates, or numbers of millionaires per 100,000 residents, or mean family income. The number of different datasets that can be mapped this way is essentially limitlesss. 
    
    The ease of grasping data mapped this way is striking. Now think of the same data on a bar graph. No meaningful relationships can pop out that way. When New Jersey and New York share similar data values on a map, it's not as conspicuous as when New York and New Mexico do. The question, "Why?" arises, followed by several others. That's a launching pad for critical thinking. We need all the critical thinking we can get.
    
    Next lesson: Greenland is WAY smaller than Africa, despite what some maps seem to show. Please alert Mr. Trump.

Many readers have commented that Florida and Texas have banned so many books and wondered why.
    Governer Ron DeSantis (R-FL) and Governor Greg Abbott (R-TX) have been very proactive about banning books they believe are harmful for children to read. 
    Florida was once a heavily Democratic state but has consistently become majority Republican in recent years due to the influx of Republicans relocating from "Blue" states like NY and California to escape high taxes, harsh NY winters, traffic, fires, earthquakes, and Democratic policies with which they disagree.
    There are some areas in Florida that are still somewhat less conservative like SE Fla, parts of Central and NE Fla but in the last few years it has turned into a "Red" state and the majority of voters elect more conservative politicians who have banned certain books from public schools.
    I am not at all surprised that Florida seems to be a leader in this movement having observed the changing demographics in the state in recent years.

comments.raw_comment:
The Restriction of Speech
    The graph, sourced by Pen America, makes it almost impossible not to wonder: what is being kept from me, and what should we keep from our youth? With such a progressive movement of silencing and removing works from states, it's easy to get lost in knowing what is right or wrong. Are these books being banned because they are bad and hurting the minds of our youth or are they being banned to push an agenda? Should Americans be letting their children read books that fill their minds with wrong things? This graph shows Florida, having Texas close behind, banning the most books. On the other hand, states like Alaska, Hawaii, Arizona, Montana, Alabama, and Nevada have no books banned. Any book can be in any of the states, so that raises the worry of why books are banned in some places and not others. When viewing this topic from the American standpoint you can stand to reason the fight for our First Amendment: the Freedom of Speech. Americans must also push to fight to keep books that may be indoctrinating youths off the shelf. Americans should have raised concerns about this drastic variety of 0 books to 6,000 being banned, so go to a local library or school board meeting to voice your concerns. This choice by states can lead to either our youth's safety or the chance of a fight regarding the want to protect one's freedoms. The choices are up to the avid reader in each state, which depending on where you are, may limit what you can access.

comments.raw_comment: After thoroughly looking into this graph, I noticed it displays information about banned books at a state level from July to December 2023. I noted that Texas and Florida had the highest number of banned books, in contrast to states with zero banned books, such as Hawaii, Nevada, New Mexico, Montana, and Alabama. This struck me as odd since a few states are in similar areas, so it’s not necessarily a contrast in location. The majority of states, however, have less than 500 banned books, which is still a lot, considering how much effort and time is put into writing a novel. This makes me wonder what content has to be in a book for it to get banned? How is it decided that documented literature can be taken away from new generations? In my freshman year, we read To Kill A Mockingbird, which is seen as controversial due to its racist language and themes. After reading this book, I felt educated on what that time period was like. It gave me and my classmates a new perspective on how people were treated then. This grasp on a previous period in human history enlightened me and showed me how different we are as a society today. America's Banned Book Controversy: Is Knowledge Power?"

comments.raw_comment:
Hiding Knowledge From Future Generations
    I notice that only eight out of the fifty states have no banned books in their scholastic libraries. This is a shockingly small number of states that give their students complete access to any books they may want to read or research. My question is, why are some states restricting access to certain books? Is it because of their controversial topics? Some of the books banned in these states are historical books that give you background knowledge about the past that is less talked about. For example, Uncle Tom’s Cabin is banned in many Southern states and their schools because of its controversial topic of slavery. I acknowledge that some books express sensitive content that school districts don’t want their kids to learn, but almost every single piece of literature should be available to young students who are learning about the past, present, and future of the world they live in. Every piece of literature ever written is or will be a part of documented history, and it isn’t right to deny future generations this history or knowledge, no matter how controversial it is.

comments.raw_comment: I notice in this graph that this information is from a very short period of time (July-December) in 2023. It is interesting that some states, such as Florida and Texas are in the dark red, indicating a high amount of banned literature, while some states have banned 0 books during this period. The dark red indicates numbers of over 3,000 books being banned in just a few months. This is very shocking and makes you wonder what qualities these works retain that creates so much controversy to the point where it needs to be completely censored from the public. I wonder if the content of these banned books is directly based on the political opinions of the state. Is it really ethical to ban books if our first amendment right–protecting our freedom of speech–is prevalent, perhaps today more than ever? This connects to my community personally because I think reading classic literature is very important, however, classic works that we have read in previous years at school are being challenged as being of controversial nature. These works include Of Mice and Men, and To Kill a Mockingjay, which both portray important themes about our society  that cannot simply be overlooked because they contain sensitive topics. I think it is important to not shield important messages from children in schools due to controversy because controversy in our world and country is unavoidable. “Should Literature be Censored in America?”

comments.raw_comment: After analyzing the graph I noticed that this data is from July to December 2023 and depicts the number of banned books per state. Florida has the highest number of books banned from around 3,0001 to 6,000 and Texas is close behind with 1,001 to 3,000. States like Arizona, Nevada, Montana, Alabama, and Hawaii have around zero. The graph depicts that typically Southeastern states seem to have more states that banned over 1 to 10 books and Northwestern states typically have a lower average. By looking at this graph it makes me wonder why books are banned and who decided what to ban. This makes me curious as to whether there are similar topics discussed in most banned books. Do different states' politics influence what books can and can't be outlawed? For example, are majority-ruled Republican states less likely to have prohibited books or the other way around? Is the government trying to hide to Americans certain subjects discussed in books and if so why? In my freshman honors English class, we read two books that are often banned in the US: To Kill a Mockingbird and Of Mice and Men. Both books described the hardships faced at that time and allowed me to gain perspective on these periods. Without the books, it would be hard to understand certain points the author made stand out about racism, sexism, and other sensitive subjects. However, sometimes the author of the book can be seen as insensitive and can personally hurt certain individuals views.

comments.raw_comment: After looking at the graph I noticed a few different things. The first thing I noticed were the seven states within the country that don’t have banned books: Arizona, Nevada, Montana, Hawaii, Connecticut, Alabama, and Delaware. I also noticed that the map is solely of the United States. Another observation I had was that Florida and Texas have the most banned books in the whole country. This makes me wonder what types of books are banned in Colorado and why they are even banned at all. I wonder what the constraints are of banned books are and what steps are taken to get a book banned in the state and why a book would even be bad enough to ban when you have the choice to read a book in the first place. This connects to me because I know that I have read banned books before within the state of Colorado, so what does it mean when a book is “banned” if students still have access to it. Not only this, but this connects to my community because how are books banned in schools supposed to be segregated from non-banned books in the community library because you can access them through your local library and then bring them on campus without ever knowing that book was banned. It also sparks the thought that many teachers or even administrators don’t know the list of banned books by memory, so how are they supposed to enforce it? A catchy headline that captures the graphs main idea is America’s Book Ban Battle of 2023: Which States Are Leading the Crackdown?

comments.raw_comment: The graph shows the number of banned books in each state across the United States. Looking closely at the graph, I notice that Texas and Florida contain the most banned books. In contrast, states such as Nevada and Arizona contain absolutely no banned books. I wonder why this may be? Is it because the state of Texas has different views and opinions than the state of Arizona? I am from Texas and seeing how we contain the second most banned books concerns me on why we are so censored. In my sophomore year of high school, we were assigned a banned book project where we were able to read and research banned books. We were able to do this project on specific books because they weren't banned in our school but they were in others. This project is on the verge of being terminated due to the fact that most of these books will no longer be allowed in our library. I believe we should be able to read what we choose and we should not be censored to the stories and ideas of creative authors but the state of Texas and many other states believe otherwise. A catchy headline for this graph could be "The Differing Ideas of Banned Books Based on The States."

Limitation of Learning
    In this graph, I immediately noticed that Texas and Florida are the states with the largest number of banned books. I wonder how 5 states have absolutely zero books banned when some novels cover very harsh or graphic subjects. This graph relates to my community because I live in Texas, and there are many books that students like myself are not permitted to read today. For example, in my English class last year every student did research on a book that was banned in another area and gave their opinion on if they agreed that it should be banned or not, and many disagreed. Therefore, there were enough books for all students to research while still having a few options left over, which can limit students' knowledge.

comments.raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I notice that the number of banned books varies greatly across states. Florida stands out with between 3,001 and 6,000 books banned represented in a dark maroon red, while states like Arizona have no banned books at all, marked in grey. Pennsylvania falls somewhere in the middle with 501 to 1,000 books banned. This suggests that while book bans aren't happening everywhere, they are particularly concentrated in states like Florida and Texas. This makes me wonder: why are Florida and Texas leading the way in banning books, and what specific criteria are being used to determine which books should be removed? How do these bans affect students’ access to diverse perspectives and the freedom to think critically? I also wonder how these book bans impact educators—are they being forced to limit their teaching materials or self-censor? In my own state, there have been only 1 to 10 banned books, which feels relatively low, but it still makes me think about the impact of censorship on access to knowledge. This issue also resonates with me because I recently wrote an essay on political courage, focusing on Congressman Jamie Raskin, who has actively opposed book bans. His argument that banning books attacks First Amendment rights and harms democracy deeply connects to the current situation. In fact, Raskin’s own book was banned in Texas, so I’ve been aware of this issue for some time.
    
    Headline: "Book Bans Surge Nationwide, with Florida and Texas Leading the Charge"

States in the midwest, plus Florida and Texas, tend to ban more books. Not much research is required to quickly determine that this is because these states in particular have a habit of restricting education, especially education relating to diversity (such as LGBTQ+ identities or cultural diversity).
         Some things that this makes me wonder are what kind of books are banned in the smaller states outside of the midwest, and what kind of books are bad enough to be able to be banned in the states with only 1-10 banned books? It's a pretty exclusive club for those states, and I wonder the prerequisites to get in.
         While brainstorming headlines, I came up with "countless books banned throughout U.S.; children's education falters." While it's a little dramatic, it describes the situation decently. And as all good journalists know, sensationalizing it will make people read it.
         I live in Vermont, so I did some research about the books banned in Vermont. It's one of those states that has very few books banned in it. I couldn't find any sources that told me which books were banned exactly, but knowing Vermont, I believe they're books that are especially against equity or diversity, and/or directly promote violence against these groups, though that's a guess.

This graph relates to my community because I live in New Jersey. New Jersey is an area with very little book banning. I think that banning some books is necessary for extreme cases. However, it should mainly try to be avoided, or else it contradicts freedom of speech and liberty. Therefore, my community and I should be grateful to live in New Jersey.
